newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Mexico blocks progress on global landmines ban.
newsitem.headline: Mexico blocks progress on global landmines ban.

text.p: Mexico on Thursday blocked a Western attempt in a U.N.-backed forum to launch negotiations towards a global ban on landmines.
Western diplomats expressed confusion and disappointment over the veto, saying it seemed to break a Mexican government pledge won by U.S. President Bill Clinton during a visit there last month.

Prospects now appeared dimmer than ever for a breakthrough during the session of the 61-member Conference on Disarmament which ends on June 27, and probably even at the final seven-week round starting in late July, they added.
The Conference has been trying to adopt its 1997 work programme since January, but remains paralysed due to a split over its priorities.
In a tactical manoeuvre, Western countries keen to start work on a ban tried to bring any objectors out into the open.
Finland, supported by Australia, Britain, France and the United States, called on any members opposed to appointing a special co-ordinator on landmines to declare so publicly.
The request was designed to embarrass non-aligned states who have been accused of obstructing progress behind the scenes.
After three hours of heated debate, Mexican ambassador Antonio de Icaza objected to the Conference president putting the Finnish question -- thereby blocking a consensus decision.
Mexico did not view the Geneva forum as the appropriate one for landmines negotiations, he said.
"Mexico blocked it. Clearly Mexico wants to be seen as a champion of nuclear disarmament and also keep mines for possible use in Chiapas," said one Western diplomat.
The state of Chiapas, one of Mexico's poorest, is home to Zapatista rebels and has been the scene of battles between radical peasants and local political bosses.
"During the debate, Cuba and Syria obviously shared Mexico's view, but didn't feel the need to stand up and be counted," another diplomat said.
Anti-personnel landmines are blamed for killing 25,000 people a year and maiming many more.

Western states are keen to launch talks on banning them in the Geneva-based Conference, in parallel to Canada's "Ottawa Process" which aims to reach a ban among some 50 countries by the end of this year.
China and Russia -- major producers and users of landmines -- are not taking part in the Canadian bid. This means a viable, universal ban could only be clinched in Geneva, diplomats say.
But non-aligned countries say top priority should be given to concrete steps towards total nuclear disarmament, and only then would they be ready to work on issues including landmines.
Mexico, speaking on behalf of the Group of 21 non-aligned countries, tabled the text of a mandate for a new committee to negotiate total nuclear disarmament within a specified time.
"The Group of 21 continues to attach the highest priority to the establishment of an ad hoc committee on nuclear disarmament," de Icaza said in a speech.
Brazil's envoy Gilberto Vergne Saboia supported the move, adding: "Nuclear disarmament is a legitimate aspiration of the international community."
The five declared nuclear states (Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States) have refused the call by non-aligned states to enter talks on total nuclear disarmament.
